categoryName: Fresh vegetable assortment for a hill township

skuLines.examples: Loose UP/Punjab table potato; HP hill potato (Lahaul/Shimla seed-belt table grade); Safal graded potato; Reliance Fresh loose potato
skuLines.packSizes: Loose 250g/500g/1kg/2kg; 5kg & 10kg poly bag; 50kg jute bag for mess/langar
skuLines.priceBand: ₹30-55/kg retail (Delhi retail 27-Aug-2026 ₹34-40; hill retail runs ~10-20% above plains)
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round. Cheapest Feb-Apr (fresh Punjab/UP crop); dearest Aug-Oct on cold-store stock
skuLines.marginBand: 5-12% (known-value item, priced to hold footfall, not to earn)
skuLines.notes: The single highest-tonnage vegetable line. Keeps 3-6 weeks in a dark, dry, ventilated hill store — Baru Sahib's cool ambient IS the cold chain for 5-6 months a year. Monsoon humidity causes sprouting and soft rot: stack in crates, never gunny on concrete. This is the line to buffer 2-3 weeks deep before the monsoon road-closure window.

skuLines.examples: Loose new-crop baby potato; baby potato 500g pack (BigBasket/Safal-style)
skuLines.seasonality: Jan-Mar only (new crop)
skuLines.notes: Very short shelf life (7-10 days), thin skin bruises on hill road transport. Order small and often; do not buffer.

skuLines.examples: Loose Nashik red onion; HP/Punjab local onion; graded 1kg onion pack
skuLines.priceBand: ₹35-85/kg (Delhi retail 27-Aug-2026 ₹55-65; news corpus shows +51% YoY spikes)
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; price peaks Aug-Nov before kharif arrival, cheapest Feb-Apr
skuLines.notes: Second-highest tonnage line. Best keeper in the whole category (4-8 weeks) which makes it the anchor of a monsoon buffer. Avoid entirely during Navratri fasting weeks for a slice of the campus — see the vrat line. Price volatility is the biggest single P&L risk in this category.

skuLines.examples: Loose small onion; pearl onion 250g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round
skuLines.notes: South Indian usage; low pull in a predominantly Punjabi/North Indian campus. Carry 5-10kg only, mainly for South Indian teaching staff. High peeling labour, so slow movement = high shrink.

skuLines.examples: Loose hybrid tomato (Solan 'red gold' belt, Nashik, Madanapalle); Safal graded tomato
skuLines.priceBand: ₹20-100/kg — the most volatile line in the store (Delhi 27-Aug-2026 only ₹22-26; wholesale up ~59% YoY in other windows)
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round need. Price spikes Jun-Aug (monsoon) and Dec-Jan (cold damage); crashes Feb-Mar and Oct-Nov
skuLines.marginBand: 8-15% (KVI), but shrink of 8-15% can erase it
skuLines.notes: Sirmaur/Solan is India's tomato belt — Solan is literally nicknamed 'City of Red Gold' — so this is the strongest LOCAL sourcing case in the whole category: ~60-70km, one hill road, no plains freight. Buy firm/pink-shoulder, never fully ripe: a fully ripe tomato will not survive 30-50km of hill road plus a day on shelf.

skuLines.examples: Loose desi (deshi) tomato; hill-grown salad tomato; local Rajgarh/Solan farm tomato
skuLines.seasonality: May-Oct from HP hill farms
skuLines.notes: Softer, thinner-skinned, better flavour — the premium tier of the same commodity, and the easiest 'grown 20km from here' story to sell on a campus. 3-5 day shelf life; sell within 48h of arrival.

skuLines.examples: Loose Himachal/Sirmaur ginger; Kerala/Meghalaya ginger; graded 200g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; fresh HP crop Oct-Dec, dearest May-Jul
skuLines.notes: Sirmaur district grows ginger commercially — direct local procurement possible. Excellent keeper (3-6 weeks in a cool dark hill store), so it buffers well against monsoon closures. Sells in ₹10-20 grammages, so keep a small-weight scale at the counter.

skuLines.examples: Loose Indian garlic (MP/Rajasthan); Himachal hill garlic; peeled garlic 100g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; new crop Mar-May is cheapest, Dec-Feb dearest
skuLines.notes: Himachal garlic has an established out-of-state market (it ships to South India), so local sourcing is realistic. Best keeper in the category — 2-4 months dry. Peeled garlic in a tub is the highest-margin sub-line but needs refrigeration and a 5-7 day sell-by.

skuLines.examples: Loose green chilli (hybrid/desi); Shimla-belt hill chilli; 100g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; dearest in monsoon
skuLines.notes: Tiny ticket (₹5-10 per purchase) but bought almost every day by almost every household — a stock-out is noticed immediately. Wilts in 3-4 days; store cool and covered, never in direct sun at the counter.

skuLines.examples: Loose kagzi lemon; hill lemon (galgal); 4-piece pack
skuLines.seasonality: Cheapest Jul-Sep; dearest Mar-Jun (peak nimbu-pani season, worst supply)
skuLines.notes: Sell by piece, not weight — that is how the customer thinks. Himachal galgal (hill lemon) is a genuine local line Nov-Feb. Keeps 2-3 weeks cool.

skuLines.examples: Loose bunch; 100g pack; hill-grown local bunch
skuLines.priceBand: ₹10-30 per bunch (₹14-17/kg wholesale-linked in Delhi 27-Aug-2026, but retail is bunch-priced)
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; scarce and dear Jun-Aug (rots in monsoon), abundant Nov-Feb
skuLines.marginBand: 35-55% (highest-margin line in the category by percentage)
skuLines.notes: Highest-frequency purchase in the whole store and the classic 'if they don't have dhania they don't have vegetables' trust signal. 2-3 day shelf life; 20-40% shrink is normal. Wrap in damp cloth, keep at 4-8°C, never stack. Ideal candidate for on-campus polyhouse growing.

skuLines.examples: Loose bunch; 100g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Mar-Jun (chutney/shikanji season); scarce in deep winter
skuLines.notes: Same fragility profile as coriander, lower volume. Grows easily on campus — the cheapest thing to stop importing over 30-50km of hill road.

skuLines.examples: Loose bunch; 250g/500g pack; hill-grown local palak
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Oct-Mar; poor and expensive Jun-Sep
skuLines.notes: The one green that matters for BOTH ends of the population: iron for adolescent hostel students and the standard first-food puree for the campus's babies. 2-4 day shelf life, very high monsoon shrink. Cool hill climate means locally grown palak is viable Sep-Apr.

skuLines.examples: Loose sarson bunch; sarson+bathua+palak saag combo bundle; ready-to-cook chopped saag pack
skuLines.seasonality: STRICTLY Nov-Feb — and in those four months it is a top-5 volume line
skuLines.notes: Non-negotiable in a Punjabi Sikh institution: makki-di-roti with sarson-da-saag is the defining winter meal, and langar kitchens buy it in quintals. The cleaning and chopping is the pain point — a pre-cleaned, pre-chopped 500g saag pack (sarson+bathua+palak in the right ratio) is the single best value-added line this store could launch, and it directly serves working staff families.

skuLines.examples: Loose methi bunch; 250g pack; kasuri-grade local methi
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Nov-Feb; thin and dear Jun-Sep
skuLines.notes: Methi-aloo, methi paratha, methi-matar-malai — core winter North Indian cooking. 2-3 day shelf life. Surplus can be sun-dried into kasuri methi and sold year-round, which turns shrink into a shelf-stable SKU.

skuLines.examples: Loose bathua bunch; saag combo bundle
skuLines.seasonality: Dec-Feb only
skuLines.notes: The third leg of authentic Punjabi saag alongside sarson and palak, and often free-foraged in hill areas — meaning very cheap local procurement from Rajgarh farmers in exactly the months when plains produce is hardest to truck in.

skuLines.line: Regional greens — amaranth (chaulai), sorrel (khatta palak), colocasia leaves (arbi patta), dill (soya)
skuLines.examples: Loose bunches, sold by the bundle
skuLines.seasonality: Chaulai Mar-Aug; arbi patta monsoon; soya and khatta palak winter
skuLines.notes: Carry 2-3 of these on rotation, not all four — each has a narrow following (regional staff, Himachali households who make patrode from arbi patta). Very high shrink if over-ordered. Best sourced entirely from local Sirmaur farmers as a same-day line.

skuLines.examples: Loose bunch; 250g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Nov-Mar
skuLines.notes: Rising fast on the back of Indo-Chinese cooking, which is exactly what a 18-25 university cohort cooks in hostel kitchens. Hill-grown quality is excellent. 4-6 day shelf life.

skuLines.examples: Loose sprigs; 50g/100g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round
skuLines.notes: Trivial rupee value, disproportionate annoyance when absent — it is not growable in a cold hill climate and there is no substitute, so residents genuinely cannot get it any other way. Keeps 1-2 weeks refrigerated in an airtight box, so it is cheap to never run out of.

skuLines.examples: Loose whole head; hill-grown Snowball/Pusa; trimmed 500g pack
skuLines.packSizes: Per piece (400g-1.2kg head); loose by weight; 500g cut pack
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Oct-Feb; HP hill crop supplies the plains Jun-Sep, so local availability is actually good in monsoon
skuLines.notes: Named in the source material as THE North Indian staple vegetable dish. Sell by piece — that is how it is bought. Himachal is a major off-season cauliflower supplier, so this is one of the few lines where the hill location is an advantage, not a penalty. 5-8 day shelf life in cool hill ambient.

skuLines.examples: Loose whole head; hill-grown cabbage; shredded 250g pack
skuLines.packSizes: Per piece (500g-2kg); loose by weight; 250g shredded pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round from HP hills; peak Nov-Feb
skuLines.notes: Best keeper among the brassicas — 2-3 weeks cool, which makes it a monsoon-buffer line. HP grows it locally at scale. Shredded pack for the hostel/salad trade carries triple the margin of the whole head.

skuLines.examples: Loose red cabbage; 250g quarter pack
skuLines.seasonality: Nov-Mar
skuLines.notes: Salad/exotic tier. Grown in the Shimla apple belt per the HP exotic-vegetable reporting, so sourceable locally. Sell as quarters — a whole head is too much for one household and drives shrink.

skuLines.examples: Loose head; 250g/500g pack; Shimla-belt hill broccoli
skuLines.seasonality: Oct-Mar peak; HP hill supply extends into summer
skuLines.notes: The gateway exotic — the one 'foreign' vegetable that has genuinely crossed into mainstream Indian household cooking, and the HP apple belt now grows it commercially (Tribune/TOI reporting on Himachal farmers switching to exotic veg for higher returns). Fragile: yellows in 3-4 days, needs 4-8°C and misting. Start with 5-10kg/week and grow with proven offtake.

skuLines.examples: Loose knol-khol with leaves; hill-grown
skuLines.seasonality: Nov-Mar
skuLines.notes: A genuine Himachali and Punjabi hill favourite that plains-focused assortments systematically miss. Both the bulb and the leaves are cooked. Very hardy, keeps 1-2 weeks — a good monsoon/winter buffer line and cheap from local farmers.

skuLines.line: Carrot — red desi (winter) and orange hybrid (year-round)
skuLines.examples: Loose red desi carrot (gajar for halwa/kanji); orange Nantes hybrid; 500g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Red desi STRICTLY Dec-Feb (gajar ka halwa and kanji season — a genuine volume spike); orange hybrid year-round
skuLines.notes: Carry BOTH types in winter — they are not substitutes: the red desi is for halwa and kanji, the orange for salad and sabzi. Also the safest baby-food vegetable (steam-and-mash) and a top salad item for hostel students. Excellent keeper, 2-3 weeks cool. Winter halwa demand around Lohri/Basant is a plannable spike.

skuLines.examples: Loose mooli with leaves; hill-grown mooli
skuLines.packSizes: Per piece / loose 500g/1kg; bunch of 3-4 with leaves
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Oct-Feb; HP hill mooli available longer
skuLines.notes: Mooli paratha is a Punjabi winter breakfast staple, and mooli is a langar-kitchen line for both the paratha and the salad plate. Sell with the leaves on — the leaves are cooked as saag and their presence is the freshness proof. Loses crispness in 4-5 days.

skuLines.examples: Loose shalgam; hill-grown
skuLines.seasonality: Dec-Feb only
skuLines.notes: Named in the Punjabi cuisine source material; shalgam-gosht is absent here (vegetarian campus) but shalgam sabzi and shalgam-in-saag are standard Punjabi winter cooking. Hardy, keeps 2 weeks. Cheap local procurement.

skuLines.examples: Loose beetroot; 500g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Nov-Mar, available year-round
skuLines.notes: Riding the juice/salad/'healthy' wave — the university cohort and health-conscious staff are the buyers. Best keeper among the roots after potato, 2-3 weeks. Sells well as a 250g pack because a household needs only one or two.

skuLines.examples: Loose fresh matar in pod; hill-grown HP matar; shelled 250g pack
skuLines.priceBand: ₹40-120/kg in pod (Delhi 27-Aug-2026 ₹68-81); shelled roughly 2.5x by weight
skuLines.seasonality: STRICTLY Nov-Feb for fresh — a top-5 volume line in those months and near-zero the rest of the year
skuLines.notes: Himachal is a major off-season pea supplier, so hill sourcing is strong and cheap in season. The shelling is the customer's real cost — a shelled/cleaned 250g pack sold at the counter is a proven high-margin conversion and exactly what a working staff family with small children will pay for. Fresh peas lose sugar within 48h of picking; buy daily, not weekly.

skuLines.line: Frozen green peas & IQF mixed vegetables
skuLines.examples: Safal frozen green peas; Sumeru mixed vegetables; ITC Master Chef frozen peas; McCain frozen mixed veg
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; demand peaks Mar-Oct when fresh peas are gone, and during monsoon road closures
skuLines.notes: This is the store's insurance policy, and the honest answer to eight months without fresh peas. Needs a working -18°C deep freezer with generator backup — in a hill township with power cuts, a freezer that thaws once has destroyed the stock and the customer's trust. India's ready-to-cook and IQF vegetable segment is documented as growing; a 30-50km-from-market township is the ideal use case.

skuLines.examples: Loose French beans; hill-grown Contender; 250g pack
skuLines.seasonality: HP hill crop Jun-Oct (off-season for the plains); plains crop Nov-Feb
skuLines.notes: One of Himachal's flagship off-season vegetables — locally abundant and cheap exactly when the plains are short, which is a real sourcing edge. Snaps and browns at the cut ends within 3-4 days; buy small and often.

skuLines.line: Cluster beans (guar), broad beans (sem), cowpea pods (lobia phali), butter beans
skuLines.examples: Loose guar phali; sem phali; lobia phali
skuLines.priceBand: ₹45-90/kg (Delhi 27-Aug-2026: cluster beans ₹52-61, broad beans ₹55-65, butter beans ₹54-64)
skuLines.seasonality: Guar Jul-Oct; sem Nov-Feb; lobia Jun-Sep
skuLines.notes: Carry one or two in season rather than all — each has a regional following (Gujarati/Rajasthani staff for guar, Punjabi households for sem). Over-ordering these is a classic shrink trap in a small captive market.

skuLines.examples: Loose tender bhindi; 250g/500g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Apr-Sep; scarce and dear Dec-Feb
skuLines.notes: Top-3 summer vegetable in North Indian households. Quality is everything — a woody bhindi will not sell at any price, so it must be bought tender and moved in 2-3 days. Bruises and blackens badly on hill-road transport; insist on crates, not sacks.

skuLines.examples: Loose long purple brinjal; hill-grown; 500g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; peak Aug-Mar
skuLines.notes: Everyday sabzi line. 5-7 day shelf life, one of the more transport-tolerant fresh lines. Keep out of direct sun — it dulls and shrivels visibly.

skuLines.examples: Loose big round brinjal; bharta baingan
skuLines.priceBand: ₹40-110/kg (Delhi 27-Aug-2026 big brinjal ₹86-101 — a significant premium over long)
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Nov-Feb (baingan bharta is a winter dish)
skuLines.notes: Baingan bharta is named in the source material as a signature Punjabi dish — the round type is not interchangeable with the long, and stocking only the long variety is a common assortment miss. Sells by piece.

skuLines.examples: Loose green capsicum; hill-grown Shimla capsicum; 250g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round from HP; the plains depend on hill supply Jun-Sep
skuLines.notes: Named 'Shimla mirch' for a reason — this is a Himachal crop, now heavily polyhouse-grown in HP, so local sourcing is strong and year-round. 7-10 day shelf life, one of the best-keeping soft vegetables.

skuLines.examples: Loose red & yellow capsicum; polyhouse HP coloured capsicum; 200g/2-piece pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round from HP polyhouses; dearest Jul-Sep
skuLines.notes: The classic polyhouse cash crop of Himachal — grown a few districts away, not imported. Highest rupee-per-kg of any regular vegetable, so a small volume adds real gross margin. Sell single pieces: a whole kilo is unaffordable for most, but one red capsicum at ₹35-50 is an easy add-on for a hostel cook or a family making pasta.

skuLines.examples: Loose ghiya; hill-grown lauki; half-cut piece
skuLines.packSizes: Per piece (500g-1.5kg); half-cut; loose by weight
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Apr-Sep; thinner Dec-Feb
skuLines.notes: The most-cooked gourd in North India and the single most important vegetable for the campus's two most vulnerable cohorts: it is the standard easy-digest food for the elderly and, steamed and mashed, one of the first solids given to Indian babies. Sell half-cut pieces — a 1.5kg lauki is too much for a two-person household, and half-cutting doubles the number of customers served from the same stock.

skuLines.examples: Loose tori; hill-grown
skuLines.seasonality: Apr-Sep
skuLines.notes: Standard light summer sabzi. Must be young — a mature tori is fibrous and unsaleable. 3-4 day shelf life, wilts fast in heat.

skuLines.examples: Loose karela (long/short type); hill-grown
skuLines.seasonality: Apr-Sep
skuLines.notes: Named in the Punjabi cuisine source material. Bought deliberately by diabetic and older residents as much as for taste — a real medical-adjacent demand on a campus with an elderly cohort. Keeps 5-7 days, better than most gourds.

skuLines.examples: Loose tinda; Punjab/hill tinda
skuLines.seasonality: May-Aug
skuLines.notes: Explicitly a Punjabi vegetable (named in the cuisine source material) and almost invisible in South/West Indian assortments — a store serving a Punjabi Sikh institution must carry it in season. Short window, buy small.

skuLines.examples: Loose pumpkin; cut wedge; whole small pumpkin
skuLines.priceBand: ₹20-45/kg (Delhi 27-Aug-2026 the cheapest line on the board at ₹26-31)
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; peak Jul-Oct
skuLines.notes: Three jobs at once: the cheapest vegetable per kilo on the board (so it matters to low-income staff), a baby-food and elderly staple, and — critically for a hill store — a keeper that lasts 4-8 weeks whole. Alongside potato, onion and ash gourd this is what a monsoon buffer is built from. Selling cut wedges instead of whole raises the realised margin substantially.

skuLines.examples: Loose ash gourd; cut wedge
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; peak Aug-Nov
skuLines.notes: The single best-keeping vegetable in the category — a whole ash gourd holds 2-4 months at hill ambient with no refrigeration at all. That makes it the ideal insurance stock for a monsoon road closure. Also the raw material for petha/halwa around festivals. Sell in wedges.

skuLines.examples: Loose desi kheera; long/English salad cucumber; polyhouse seedless cucumber
skuLines.packSizes: Loose 250g/500g; per piece for the long type
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Mar-Sep; year-round from HP polyhouses
skuLines.notes: Highest-frequency salad and snack item for the 5-25 age bulk of this campus — a residential school and a university hostel eat enormous quantities of plain cucumber. Carry both tiers: cheap desi kheera by weight for households and messes, and the premium seedless for the salad trade. 5-7 day shelf life, keep cool and out of the sun.

skuLines.examples: Loose zucchini; HP polyhouse zucchini; 500g pack
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round from HP polyhouses; peak Oct-Mar
skuLines.notes: Named in the reporting on Himachal and Nilgiris farmers switching to exotic vegetables, so it is now an Indian-grown line, not an import. Buyers are the university cohort cooking pasta and grills, plus staff who have lived in cities. Start with 5kg/week.

skuLines.examples: Loose arbi (small/large type); hill-grown arbi
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Jun-Oct
skuLines.notes: Named in the Punjabi cuisine source material (arbi is a standard sabzi), and Himachal households also use the leaves for patrode. Hardy tuber, keeps 1-2 weeks. A good local Sirmaur procurement line.

skuLines.examples: Loose shakarkandi; orange-flesh variety
skuLines.seasonality: Peak Oct-Feb (roasted shakarkandi is a winter street food); also a fasting staple
skuLines.notes: Three demand streams: winter roasted snack for students, baby-food puree, and one of the vegetables explicitly permitted during Hindu fasting (confirmed in the Indian cuisine source material) — which matters twice a year at Navratri. Keeps 2-4 weeks dry.

skuLines.examples: Loose elephant foot yam, cut pieces
skuLines.seasonality: Oct-Feb, with a spike at Diwali (a traditional Diwali vegetable in parts of North India)
skuLines.notes: Narrow following but a very long keeper (4-8 weeks), so the shrink risk of carrying it is low. Sold as cut pieces because a whole yam is 3-6kg.

skuLines.line: Fasting / vrat vegetables — raw banana, water chestnut (singhara), arbi, cucumber
skuLines.examples: Loose raw banana (kachcha kela); fresh singhara in season; vrat-day counter bundle
skuLines.seasonality: Two hard spikes: Chaitra Navratri (Mar-Apr) and Sharad Navratri (Sep-Oct); singhara Oct-Dec
skuLines.notes: On fasting days a slice of the campus needs vegetables that are permitted AND needs no onion or garlic at all — potato, sweet potato, raw banana, singhara, cucumber, pumpkin. The source material confirms potato and sweet potato as fasting-permitted. Build a small physical 'vrat counter' for those nine days rather than expecting customers to hunt; it is the cheapest goodwill in the calendar and it stops a trip to town.

skuLines.examples: Loose sweet corn cob (bhutta); sweet corn kernels 200g pack; baby corn 200g pack
skuLines.packSizes: Cob per piece; 200g kernel pack; baby corn 200g
skuLines.seasonality: Roasted bhutta Jun-Sep (a monsoon hill-station ritual); sweet corn and baby corn year-round
skuLines.notes: Roasted corn in the monsoon is close to a cultural default at a cold, rainy hill location — an easy impulse line at the fruits-and-vegetables counter or the canteen. Baby corn serves the Indo-Chinese cooking that the university cohort does. Corn loses sugar within 24-48h of picking, so buy daily in season.

skuLines.examples: Loose white button mushroom; 200g punnet (Solan-grown); Himalayan/Solan farm mushroom
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round from controlled growing; best quality Oct-Mar
skuLines.notes: The strongest local-sourcing story in the entire category: Solan — roughly 60-70km away — is India's 'Mushroom City' and hosts the national Directorate of Mushroom Research. Fresh, same-day mushroom at a price no plains retailer can match is a genuine competitive asset for this store. But it is also the most perishable line here: 3-4 days at 2-4°C, and it browns and slimes fast without refrigeration. Do not stock it without a working chiller.

skuLines.line: Exotic / speciality mushroom — oyster, milky, shiitake, enoki
skuLines.examples: Oyster mushroom 200g pack; milky mushroom; dried shiitake
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round
skuLines.notes: Speciality mushrooms are a documented growth segment. Solan proximity makes fresh oyster mushroom realistic. Very thin following on this campus — carry it dried (shelf-stable, no shrink) before you carry it fresh. Oyster mushroom is also a plausible on-campus cultivation project on paddy straw.

skuLines.examples: Iceberg lettuce head; romaine; 200g washed salad leaf pack
skuLines.seasonality: Oct-Mar; HP hill supply extends it
skuLines.notes: Real demand, small volume — burger/wrap/salad cooking among the 18-25 cohort. Extremely fragile: bruises in transit, browns at the cut in 2-3 days, needs 2-5°C. The cool hill climate is actually ideal for growing it, so an on-campus or nearby-farm supply is a better answer than trucking it 50km. Carry 5-10 heads and let demand prove itself.

skuLines.line: Exotic herbs — celery, parsley, basil, rosemary, thyme, leek
skuLines.examples: Celery stalk bunch; flat parsley 50g; sweet basil 50g; leek per piece
skuLines.packSizes: 50-100g pack; celery bunch; leek per piece
skuLines.priceBand: ₹40-120 per 50-100g pack; celery ₹45-100/kg (Delhi 27-Aug-2026 curry leaves ₹42-49 as a reference for bunched herbs)
skuLines.seasonality: Oct-Mar
skuLines.notes: Lowest-priority tier in the category — a handful of buyers at most on a 5,000-person campus. Value here is signalling ('they have everything') rather than volume. Herbs grow well in a cool hill climate in pots; a small on-campus herb bed would serve this line better than procurement.

skuLines.examples: Loose cherry tomato; 200g punnet; HP polyhouse cherry tomato
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round from HP polyhouses
skuLines.notes: Polyhouse-grown in Himachal, so locally available. Sells to salad-makers and to families with small children (they get eaten raw like fruit). Punnet format only — loose cherry tomatoes get squeezed and burst at a counter.

skuLines.line: Seasonal preserve vegetables — raw mango, amla
skuLines.examples: Loose raw mango (kairi) for chutney/panna/pickle; loose amla for murabba/pickle/juice
skuLines.seasonality: Raw mango Apr-Jun (aam panna and the annual pickle-making window); amla Oct-Feb
skuLines.notes: These are bought once a year in 5-20kg lots, not weekly — annual pickle and murabba making is a real household event in North Indian families, and missing the two-to-three-week window means every staff household makes a trip to town for it. Amla also has a strong Ayurvedic/health pull with the elderly. Plan these as a dated campaign, not as shelf stock.

skuLines.examples: Chopped mix-veg 500g; cleaned & chopped saag pack 500g; peeled ghiya/pumpkin cubes 400g; shelled peas 250g; grated carrot/beetroot 200g
skuLines.priceBand: ₹30-90 per pack (a 30-60% premium over the loose weight equivalent)
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; the saag pack peaks Nov-Feb, mix-veg peaks in exam and festival weeks
skuLines.marginBand: 35-50% — the highest-margin fresh format in the store
skuLines.notes: Cut and chopped vegetables are documented as the fastest-growing fresh format in Indian retail, and the fit here is unusually good: married staff with small children and babies, plus hostel kitchens, are exactly the buyers who pay for prep labour. It also converts today's near-shrink stock into a premium SKU instead of a write-off. Hard requirements: potable-water washing, food-grade gloves, a chiller at 4°C, same-day date labelling, and a same-day sell-by — cut vegetables spoil in hours, not days, and a single food-safety incident on a school campus is not recoverable.

skuLines.examples: Ready salad kit 250g (lettuce+cucumber+carrot+cherry tomato+dressing); fresh moong/moth sprouts 200g; microgreens 50g tray
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round; peaks in summer and in exam months
skuLines.notes: Sprouts are the practical half of this line and the microgreens the aspirational half. Sprouts need no cold chain to produce — they can be grown on campus in trays in 2-3 days from moong the store already sells, which makes this the rare fresh line with local production, near-zero freight, and a 40%+ margin. Sprouts must be sold within 2 days and kept cold; they are a known food-safety risk if mishandled.

skuLines.examples: Weekly organic basket (6-8 seasonal vegetables); certified organic potato/onion/tomato; local Sirmaur natural-farming produce
skuLines.priceBand: ₹300-700 per weekly basket; 40-100% premium on individual lines
skuLines.seasonality: Year-round, assortment rotates with season
skuLines.notes: Organic demand in India is rising but availability in ordinary retail shops remains thin, so there is room. On this campus the persuasive claim is not the certificate — it is 'residue-free, grown in Sirmaur, for your children'. That lands with parents of small children and babies far harder than a price argument. Run it as a pre-booked subscription so there is no unsold organic stock, which is what usually kills the line.

skuLines.priceBand: ₹40-90/kg (Delhi 27-Aug-2026: drumstick ₹61-72, ivy gourd ₹45-53, snake gourd ₹48-57, banana flower ₹22-26)

skuLines.notes: Carried for the South and East Indian teaching staff — a small cohort at a national institution, but one with no alternative source at all within 50km. Two or three of these on rotation, in small quantities, on request. Drumstick is the one with the widest following and is also used medicinally.

trends2026: Exotic vegetables have stopped being an import line and become a Himachal crop. Reporting through 2025-26 covers HP farmers in the Shimla apple belt switching to broccoli, zucchini, coloured capsicum, lettuce and cherry tomato for higher returns, with the same shift in Kashmir, the Nilgiris and Prayagraj; market trackers put the exotic-vegetable segment at a ~14% CAGR. For a Sirmaur store this flips exotics from a 300km freight problem into a local sourcing opportunity.

Cut, washed and chopped vegetables are the fastest-growing fresh format in India (BusinessLine reports farms restructuring to supply the cut-and-chopped boom), pulled by working households and small kitchens. It carries roughly double the margin of loose produce and converts near-shrink stock into a premium SKU.

Polyhouse and protected cultivation have scaled sharply in India, Himachal included, plus a visible hydroponics wave (Eeki Foods selling at mandi rates, restaurant-attached farms in Kerala, state polyhouse schemes). This is what now makes year-round tomato, capsicum, cucumber and exotics possible from hill farms instead of plains trucking.

Extreme vegetable price volatility is the dominant story of 2025-26: tomato wholesale up ~59% YoY in one window, onion up 51%, then crashes of up to 80% since January deepening farm distress, with monsoon and fuel-price shocks named as drivers. A single-store captive market has to decide deliberately whether to pass through spikes or smooth them.

Frozen and IQF vegetables plus ready-to-cook have moved from convenience to substitution — Indian coverage links their growth to LPG cost, small kitchens and working households, and the IQF vegetable market is tracked separately now. In a road-closure-prone hill township frozen peas and mixed veg are supply insurance, not a luxury.

Quick commerce has reset expectations even where it does not deliver. Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart have trained Indian consumers on 200-500g packs, visible grading and same-day freshness; residents of a township those apps do not serve still benchmark the local store against them, so small-pack formats and dated freshness matter more than they did three years ago.

Climate stress in the Himalayas is now named as an agricultural and logistics risk, not a weather story — rain hitting Himachal vegetable yields and pushing prices up, roads in Lahaul-Spiti washed away leaving farmers unable to reach market, and Mongabay/Dialogue Earth coverage of erratic weather in the northern Himalayas. Reliability of supply, not price, is becoming the differentiator for a hill retailer.

Organic and residue-free produce demand keeps rising while actual availability in ordinary Indian retail shops stays thin (The India Forum). The claim that converts is provenance and residue-free for children, not certification — which is precisely the pitch that works on a residential-school campus.
adjacentServices: Pre-cleaned and pre-chopped prep counter — chopped mix-veg, cleaned winter saag (sarson+bathua+palak in the right ratio), shelled peas, peeled gourd cubes, grated carrot. Highest-margin fresh format available and the exact pain point for married staff with small children. Requires potable-water washing, a 4°C chiller, gloves, and same-day date labels.

Next-day indent supply for the two canteens, the school mess and the langar kitchen — a standing kitchen indent sheet in, graded vegetables out at a fixed rate for the week. Converts the store's most volatile category into forecastable volume and takes the mess buyer off the 30-50km road.

Weekly vegetable basket subscription with doorstep drop to married staff quarters — pre-booked, pre-paid, fixed rupee value with a rotating seasonal mix. Pre-booking is what makes the organic and exotic tiers viable, because nothing is bought that is not already sold.

Direct procurement from Rajgarh and Sirmaur farmers — tomato (Solan is India's tomato belt), ginger, garlic, peas, French beans, cauliflower, knol-khol, bathua, mushroom from the Solan cluster. Cuts freight, cuts transit damage, and plugs the wallet leak that a trip to town represents.

Fresh mushroom tie-up with the Solan cluster (roughly 60-70km, and home to the national Directorate of Mushroom Research) — same-day button and oyster mushroom at a price and freshness no plains retailer can match.

On-campus growing for the lines that cannot survive the hill road — a small polyhouse or herb bed and tray-grown sprouts for coriander, mint, spring onion, lettuce, microgreens and moong sprouts. These are the highest-shrink, highest-margin lines in the category and the cool hill climate suits every one of them.

Seasonal preserve campaigns on a dated calendar — raw mango for pickle and aam panna (Apr-Jun), amla for murabba (Oct-Feb), sun-dried kasuri methi and sukha saag from winter surplus. Bulk 5-20kg lots booked in advance, which turns a once-a-year town trip into an in-campus event and turns shrink into shelf-stable stock.

A physical vrat counter for the nine days of each Navratri — potato, sweet potato, raw banana, singhara, cucumber, pumpkin grouped together, with no onion or garlic on that table. Two weeks a year, near-zero cost, disproportionate goodwill.

Daily rate board plus a WhatsApp price and arrivals list — in a captive single-store market published prices are the cheapest way to buy trust, and the arrivals note is what pulls people to the counter on the day the fragile lines land.

Monsoon buffer pack — a pre-built 10-15kg assortment of the four true keepers (potato, onion, pumpkin, ash gourd) plus frozen peas, sold ahead of a forecast road closure. Turns the store's biggest operational risk into a planned sale.

Vegetable waste routed to campus composting, biogas or dairy feed — a fresh counter generates 8-15% trim and shrink daily, and on a closed campus that has an on-site destination rather than a disposal cost.

Weighing, cutting and carry service at the counter — halving gourds and pumpkins, cutting ash gourd wedges, and free-piece cutting. Doubles the number of households one large vegetable can serve and directly lifts realised margin on the cheapest lines.
